source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Origin of RPD: Klein, Calderwood and Clinton-Cirocco (1986) studied fireground commanders. The first hypothesis was that commanders compare a pair of options. It was wrong. They usually generated one option and needed no more.
numbers: Commanders drew on a repertoire built over more than a decade of real and virtual experience. Second-hand account of the 1986 study; no counts given here.
limits: Describes the study as summarised by the authors, not the raw data. Counts (commanders, decisions) are not in this text.
agent_relevance: Our agent can default to one plausible candidate first, then test it, instead of listing many options.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: RPD loop as Kahneman and Klein state it: pick the first plausible option, simulate it (progressive deepening, deGroot 1946/1978), implement if it works, modify if it has flaws, else go to the next most plausible option.
numbers: Order of steps: generate one, simulate, accept or modify, then next option. Replicated in system design, military command and control, and offshore oil installation management (Klein 1998 review, cited).
limits: Replication claims are by the model's authors and rest on their own cited review. The next-option step makes this a serial generate-test loop, not a single guess.
agent_relevance: Maps onto a generate-then-check loop with a ranked candidate queue; G3 requires the check be real, which mental simulation alone is not.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: The 1989 NDM meeting: 30 researchers who studied decisions in natural settings (firefighters, nuclear plant controllers, Navy and Army officers, highway engineers) met for several days. Book: Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok 1993.
numbers: Group size 30. Lipshitz (1993) listed field models: RPD, cognitive continuum (Hammond et al. 1987), image theory (Beach 1990), dominance search (Montgomery 1993), skills-rules-knowledge and decision ladder (Rasmussen 1986).
limits: Defines NDM by setting, not by one mechanism; several competing field models exist.
agent_relevance: Mode choice: our states could pick among rival modes (recognise, diagnose, compare), as these models do.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: The key boundary condition: intuition is skilled only if (1) the environment has valid, learnable cues and (2) the person had enough opportunity to learn them. Subjective confidence is not a reliable sign of accuracy.
numbers: Two conditions. Chess masters estimated at 10,000 hours (Chase and Simon 1973). Valid cues must exist 'at least in principle', even if the expert cannot state them.
quote: Skilled intuitions will only develop in an environment of sufficient regularity, which provides valid cues to the situation.
limits: Qualitative argument, not a measured effect. Validity of an environment is hard to judge in advance (Tetlock 2005 case).
agent_relevance: Gate intuition mode on a validity check of the task domain. An LLM has seen many regular domains but gets no feedback inside the run.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Fractionated expertise: Shanteau (1992) found expertise in livestock judges, astronomers, test pilots, chess masters, physicists, accountants, grain inspectors, photo interpreters, insurance analysts. Poor performance in stockbrokers, clinical psychologists, psychiatrists, admissions officers, court judges, personnel selectors, intelligence analysts.
numbers: Nurses, physicians and auditors were on both lists. Predictors: predictability of outcomes, amount of experience, quality of feedback, static versus dynamic stimuli.
quote: fractionation of expertise is the rule, not an exception
limits: List-based; Shanteau's lists are second-hand here. No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Competence is task-slice specific. Our agent should not assume reliable intuition across a whole domain.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: The competing tradition: Meehl (1954) found statistical rules beat clinicians in nearly every study reviewed. Goldberg (1970): bootstrap models of 29 clinicians on 861 patient MMPI profiles were almost always more accurate than the clinicians they modelled.
numbers: Goldberg: 29 judges, 861 cases, 11 scales. Karelaia and Hogarth (2008) meta-analysis supports the bootstrap effect and ties it to inconsistency (noise).
limits: Older studies, mostly lab-style cue-to-criterion tasks, not the fast dynamic tasks NDM studies.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: code, not judgment, should do ranking when cues are stable and noise is the main risk.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Dual-process fit: the authors say RPD has an automatic part that brings candidates to mind (System 1) and a deliberate part, mental simulation of the candidate (System 2). System 2 can override intuition when cues say it may be wrong.
numbers: Described as a shared view of both camps. No numbers.
limits: Mapping is conceptual. Simulation in humans is also fast and partly intuitive, so the split is not clean.
agent_relevance: Gives the right division of labour: model proposes, program checks. Matches our schema roles.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Premortem (Klein 2007): the team imagines the plan has failed and writes the reasons in two minutes; the facilitator takes reasons round the table starting with the leader. Rests on prospective hindsight (Mitchell, Russo, Pennington 1989).
numbers: Two-minute writing step. Both authors endorse it as a semi-formal debiasing method.
limits: Authors give no outcome data for the premortem here.
agent_relevance: A cheap 'assume it failed, list causes' step, but G1 says only on a signal, so trigger it on a failed check.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: from theory to toolbox
finding: History of NDM: 1989 workshop of roughly 30 researchers; book Decision Making in Action in 1993; HFES NDM technical group in 1995; 12 NDM conferences by 2016. The Vincennes incident (an AEGIS cruiser shot down an Iranian airliner) helped drive Navy interest.
numbers: About 30 researchers, 1989. RPD said to cover 80 to 90 percent of firefighter decisions. Depends on 10 to 20 years of experience.
limits: The 80-90 percent figure is stated without a table; the original 1986 count is not shown here. Authors are the model's originators.
agent_relevance: The 80-90 percent is the number to test an LLM against: does it also mostly take one option and act?

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: from theory to toolbox
finding: Critique on record: Lipshitz, Klein, Orasanu and Salas (2001) 'Taking stock of NDM' drew 16 commentaries. Lab researchers said NDM needed more rigour and controlled methods. NDM authors call the lack of correct answers and hypothesis testing 'Guilty as charged'.
numbers: 16 commentaries. Macrocognition split off from microcognition around 2000; NDM broadened into macrocognition about 2003.
limits: Authors' own summary of a debate, so weighted toward NDM. No quantitative counter-evidence cited.
agent_relevance: RPD is mainly descriptive with little prediction. Treat it as a design pattern, not a validated causal law.

source: Klein et al. (2016) Can we trust best practices? Six cognitive challenges of evidence-based approaches
finding: Klein et al. restate the boundary: intuitions are useful under two conditions, a reasonably stable environment and chances to learn from feedback. Stock selection fails both; medicine meets both partly; chess meets both strongly.
numbers: Two conditions. Chess pattern store: tens of thousands of patterns (Chase and Simon 1973). Medicine is 'not a zero-reliability domain'.
limits: Position paper with no new data. Same camp as the model's authors.
agent_relevance: Good for tagging task types as high-validity, mixed or zero-validity, which decides how much to trust first-pass answers.

source: Klein et al. (2016) The ShadowBox approach to cognitive skills training: an empirical evaluation
finding: Hintze (2008) fireground training test: fire officers did scenarios and saw an expert panel's rankings and reasons. After one day the feedback group scored 86.9 against 73.6 for 15 controls without feedback, an 18 percent gap.
numbers: F = 14.09, p < .001. Scored as match to expert panel ranking on scenario 4. Starting scores were not controlled.
limits: Match to experts is not job performance. No baseline adjustment.
agent_relevance: Learning from expert reasons, not only expert answers, is a trainable route; for us it hints at storing worked cases with rationale.

source: Klein et al. (2016) The ShadowBox approach to cognitive skills training: an empirical evaluation
finding: Evaluation 1, US Marines (N = 59, Camp Pendleton and Camp Lejeune): the SME-feedback group (n = 29) matched the expert panel better at Time 4 than the no-feedback group.
numbers: M = .59 (SD .23) versus M = .44 (SD .24); t(58) = 2.45, p = .02; d = .63. Groups equal at Time 1: t(58) = .98. About 3 hours. Counterbalanced orders ABCD and DCBA.
limits: Single study by the method's developers; outcome is agreement with experts; no on-the-job test.
agent_relevance: Moderate effect from seeing experts' reasons; an in-context example with rationale helps pattern matching.

source: Klein et al. (2016) The ShadowBox approach to cognitive skills training: an empirical evaluation
finding: Evaluation 2, 30 Army second lieutenants, no control group: alignment with experts rose from M = .48 (SD .21) at Time 1 to M = .58 (SD .19) at Time 4.
numbers: 21 percent gain; t(29) = -2.10, p = .04; d = .38. 20 of 30 improved (mean gain 55 percent); 10 got worse (mean fall 36 percent). Under 1 hour.
limits: No control group, no counterbalancing. One third got worse. Small N.
agent_relevance: Expert exposure can hurt a third of learners; our agent should check, not assume, that a stored pattern helps.

source: Flin et al. (2007) How do surgeons make intraoperative decisions?
finding: Four decision modes in surgery: intuitive (recognition-primed), rule-based, option comparison, creative. Surgeons' interview accounts showed intuitive decisions; they rarely described rule lookup; creative decisions were not mentioned.
numbers: Cites Way et al.: 252 laparoscopic bile duct injuries were mostly perceptual (misjudged situation), not skill or judgment errors. Police assess operational situations in under 3 minutes (cited).
limits: Conceptual review; no counts of surgeon decisions by mode in the opened text; participant number not given.
agent_relevance: Errors cluster in situation assessment, not in choosing the action. Put checks on the diagnosis step.

source: Yu (2016) Stress potentiates decision biases: SIDI model
finding: SIDI model: stress cuts prefrontal control and shifts decisions toward fast habit or emotion. Intuitive output can become the final decision without being checked.
numbers: Directional evidence only: stressed participants kept actions after outcome devaluation (Schwabe and Wolf 2009); cortisol impaired cognitive reflection test scores (Margittai 2015); stress produced premature decisions before alternatives were seen (Keinan 1987).
limits: Few effect sizes or sample sizes in text; the author says the model risks being circular and effects vary by stress type, sex, timing. Covers reward-based decisions only.
agent_relevance: Pressure is where recognition mode wins and checking is skipped. Our program should force the check step under budget pressure.

source: Baldwin et al. (2022) A reasonable officer: stress, training and performance in a realistic scenario
finding: N = 122 Canadian police officers, one realistic lethal-force scenario (mean 9 min 25 s). 34 officers (27.9 percent) made at least one lethal-force error: 20 (16.4 percent) shot a bystander with a cellphone, 9 (7.4 percent) shot a knife-holding subject threatening self-harm, 5 (4.1 percent) both.
numbers: Overall performance mean 59 percent (about 50 novice to 74 elite). Each training level about +3 points (beta = 0.461, p < .001). Each service year about -0.39 points (p = .026). Higher critical-phase SNS predicted lower score (B = -0.571, p = .027). R2 = 0.30. Peak HR about 150 bpm vs 75 rest. Shooting the subject: OR 1.374 per training level, 1.119 per service year.
limits: Single scenario, no low-stress control, one agency, no backup, years of service is a crude measure. Authors read the errors as RPD misdiagnosis under stress; this is an interpretation, not a test.
agent_relevance: A failed-recognition case: a fast schema match gave the wrong action. More training raised one error type, so recognition can lock in a wrong frame.

source: Le Menn et al. (2019) Handball goalkeeper decisions through the RPD lens
finding: Case study of one elite handball goalkeeper, 26 shot sequences, 83 coded decision accounts, using RPD levels. Simple match 38 (46 percent), simulation 28 (34 percent), diagnosis 17 (20 percent).
numbers: Salient features 419 units: relevant cues 185 (44 percent), expectancies 93 (22 percent), actions 74 (18 percent). Rater agreement 85 percent (features), 95 percent (processes). Level did not vary with distance: chi2(2) = 1.044, p = .593; micro-decision did: chi2(3) = 26.53.
limits: N = 1 player, retrospective video-cued recall. Simple match was 60-81 percent in other team sports, so this goalkeeper is a lower outlier.
agent_relevance: Mode mix is task-dependent, not fixed at 80 percent. Our agent should expect to switch modes by situation.

source: Macquet (2020) review, as cited in a sport RPD perspective (Frontiers 2022)
finding: Across sport studies, 60 to 81 percent of expert decisions were simple match, 13 to 28 percent diagnosis, and 3 to 24 percent evaluating a course of action. Experts chose the preferred first option in about 80 percent of decisions (no citation given).
numbers: Ranges from Macquet (2020) via a secondary narrative review. Klatt et al. 2019: creativity score correlates with first-option quality. Collins et al. 2016: coaches under less time pressure made more analytic decisions than athletes.
limits: Second-hand figures; 80 percent claim uncited; most work qualitative or case-based; sport only. Evidence for an intuitive-analytic continuum is inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain replication of the first-option pattern, with time pressure and role changing the mode.

source: Collins, Collins & Carson (2016) If it feels right, do it: intuitive decision making in high-level coaches
finding: 18 coaches (8 rugby union, 10 adventure sport), critical-decision-method interviews. All 18 reported intuitive decisions. 12 of 18 used an 'audit', checking whether intuition and analysis agreed.
numbers: Self-estimated intuition share: rugby about 30 percent (range 5-40); one adventure coach 90 percent. 12/18 audit (8/10 adventure, 4/8 rugby). Creativity named by 14 of 18. Cross-check on 20 percent of transcripts.
limits: Self-report, all male British, personal-contact recruitment, crude percentage question. Planning stages were more deliberate.
agent_relevance: Practitioners blend modes: intuit, then audit. Same pattern as generate then check.

source: Systematic review of player decision making in team sports (2021)
finding: 53 studies, 2,078 participants (2,021 players, 57 coaches). Only four studied RPD directly, each with 7 to 23 participants. Ten studies were NDM-framed, 25 information-processing, 18 ecological dynamics.
numbers: Musculus (169 male soccer players): fewer options linked to a more accurate first response. Basevitch: intuition was better when time was short, more options helped when time was longer. Klatt: Brazilian players made more options and had a more accurate first option.
limits: No formal quality appraisal; many lab-based or decontextualised tasks; counts partly inconsistent; only the first part of the paper was read.
agent_relevance: Direct RPD tests are few and tiny. The 'few options, first is best' result depends on time available.

source: Shin (2019) Reasoning processes in clinical reasoning (narrative review)
finding: Review maps RPD onto medicine: typical cases get pattern recognition, atypical cases get extra cues plus hypothesis testing, cases with no prior experience get mental simulation. Dual-process view puts System 2 on when no clear pattern is found.
numbers: No quantitative data in the paper. Says the novice-deductive, expert-inductive split 'may be too conclusive'.
limits: No data; the recommendation to favour pattern reasoning rests on time limits and argument, not trials.
agent_relevance: The three RPD variants give a decision rule for mode: match, then diagnose, then simulate.

source: Danial et al. (2019) On the realization of the recognition-primed decision model for artificial agents
finding: Computational RPD: a Markov logic network trained on 17 participants' data in a virtual offshore platform with FIRE and EVACUATE situations, plus ontology-based reasoning, inside a BDI agent. Data split 80 percent training, 20 percent test.
numbers: 17 participants, 2 situations each. Reviews earlier models: C-RPD in UML (Nowroozi), BDI-RPD (Norling), R-CAST (Fan et al.), Bayesian-network pilot model (Hu et al.), Sokolowski's military model.
limits: The text calls Klein's model qualitative and says it does not specify methods for decisions or planning. Authors criticise C-RPD for not saying how actions are evaluated. Accuracy figures were not found in the parts read.
agent_relevance: RPD has no standard algorithm; we must choose our own for recognition, expectancy check and simulation.

source: Danial et al. (2019) On the realization of the recognition-primed decision model for artificial agents
finding: Three RPD variants as defined in the text: (1) simple match: situation familiar, cues, goals, expected outcome and action known. (2) diagnosis: cues unclear, build a story by mental simulation when an expectancy is violated. (3) evaluate action by simulating it.
numbers: Expectancy violation triggers diagnosis. Four by-products of recognition: expectancies, relevant cues, plausible goals, action list.
limits: Description of the model, not a test.
agent_relevance: Clear state machine: recognise, check expectancies, on violation diagnose, else simulate and act. Fits our states and the anomaly signal in G1.

source: Heander et al. (2025) Code review as decision-making: a cognitive model from the questions asked
finding: Think-aloud and interview study of 10 software developers on real code reviews (34 sessions). Questions coded into 1,159 segments: 27 percent orientation, 73 percent analysis. The authors map orientation to the first half of the RPD model and analysis to a full RPD cycle.
numbers: 10 participants, mean 8 years review experience. 26 of 34 reviews got a vote of at least +1. 60 percent of sessions started by selecting which change to review. Understanding implementation 26 percent, selecting next action 15 percent.
limits: Qualitative, one company, Sweden, 10 people. Mapping to RPD is the authors' reading, not a test of RPD predictions.
agent_relevance: Code review as RPD gives a human template for an agent that reviews code: orient first, then analyse, then act on cue mismatch.

source: Kaempf, Klein, Thordsen & Wolf (1996) Decision making in complex naval command-and-control environments
finding: AEGIS combat information center officers: a search-result abstract record says recognitional strategies drove 95 percent of actions and multiple options were compared in only 4 percent. I did not open the paper.
numbers: 95 percent recognitional, 4 percent option comparison (from the abstract record only). Most decisions concerned situation assessment and diagnosis.
limits: Not verified in the full text; a blog also gave 78 and 87 percent figures that the abstract does not support. Check against the paper before use.
agent_relevance: Key replication of RPD in a military team setting, if confirmed.

source: Klein, Calderwood & Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fireground
finding: Founding study. A search summary says 26 experienced commanders (average 23 years) were interviewed on 156 decision points. Another summary puts RPD use at 80 to 90 percent. DTIC and journal copies could not be retrieved, so these numbers are unverified here.
numbers: 26 commanders, 156 decision points, 80-90 percent RPD (all unverified). Published in HFES 30th Annual Meeting proceedings, vol 1, pp 576-580.
limits: Not opened. Counts must be checked in the original; the design has no comparison group and relies on retrospective interview.
agent_relevance: Founding numbers for the one-option claim; verify before citing in a spec.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices
finding: Take-the-first heuristic in handball: only the bibliography page could be opened; no abstract there. A search result says a 2007 follow-up found the first option generated was generally better than later ones, with few options generated.
numbers: Citation: OBHDP 91(2), 215-229. No numbers retrieved.
limits: Not opened; do not cite numbers. Sport tasks with expert players only.
agent_relevance: Direct test of 'first option is good'; fetch full text in the next pass.
